newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - N.Ireland Elec steady under scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - N.Ireland Elec steady under scrutiny.

text.p: British regional electricity company (Rec) Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) turned in steady half year results on Thursday and said it hoped re-focusing its business would deliver efficiencies.

The company, whose prices are under review by British authorities, said half year pretax profits rose to 52 million pounds ($85.89 million) from 47.7 million pounds previously and paid out a dividend of 5.5 pence, up from five pence.
It said the price review by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) would "have an impact on our future income."
But chief executive Patrick Haren told Reuters in an interview that "no matter what the outcome, we will be looking for efficiency gains."
He added that NIE was hoping for "a reasonably fair outcome to give an incentive to continue driving the company to efficiences."
Shares in the company edged down 1/2p pence to 364 pence as the results were in line with expectations of profits between 46.5 million and 56 million pounds.
"It is a fairly steady set of results, no particular news, no surprises nor disappointments," Haren said.
Analysts had been expecting NIE to keep a low profile in these results while its dispute with regulator Ofreg over pricing is being considered by the MMC.

Ofreg proposed new pricing controls for the company which would have become effective in April but NIE countered with its own proposals and the matter is now being considered by the MMC, which is due to report by March 17.
Haren said the company wanted an indication from authorities as to whether it should continue planned levels of investment.
"The regulator in his price proposals signalled his view tht we should not maintain those levels," he said.
NIE had planned to spend 400 million pounds over the next five years on infrastructure and other investments, he said.
"We are an isolated system and cannot be expected to achieve similar tariffs to the UK companies which have the benefits of economy of scale and diversification of generation source," Haren added.
He said the company had already cut staff by 34 percent since privatisation five years ago.
Sales, meanwhile, are growing at a rate of around 2.9 percent, the company said, reflecting "good economic performance in the region."
It added that it remained committed "to providing the electricity infrastructure necessary to support continued growth in the Northern Ireland economy." ($1=.6054 Pound)
